zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after reading the scan: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription corrections and English review notes here are this review's scan-based work, not a replacement transcription supplied by NINJAL.

runs.text: agoa não cabe em hum vaſo. ¶

lines.note: The opening continues the preceding page's vessel comparison. The new example is explained below as torment by water, fire, and sword; its Japanese compound crosses the physical line break.
Xetno completes the compound begun with tǒ-; xeme denotes torment or punishment. The capital T in Tormento corrects OCR Formento.
Espada completes the list of means of torment, specifically the sword. This short continuation is not part of the watermelon entry below.
Suika is glossed as watermelon. The physically displaced real at the right completes the following entry's royal banner, not this fruit gloss; its opening parenthesis is retained separately.
This distinct suikwa is identified by ten'oo no hata, a royal banner or standard. The gloss's real is printed at the preceding row's right edge; Tenvǒno retains its visible v.
Suikwa no choo denotes the king's pavilion or canopy. It continues the royal-regalia vocabulary rather than the earlier watermelon sense.
Suiran is described as a herb resembling indigo. The comparison alone does not warrant assigning a modern botanical species.
Suiren is equated with kawadachi and explained as swimming or diving well. The divided Portuguese mergu- continues on the next row.
Suiren wo eta hito describes a person proficient in swimming. The gloss first completes mergulhar bem, then begins homem across the next break.

runs.text: mem destro em nadar, paßar o rio, &c.

lines.note: The proficient person can swim and cross a river. Destro is the historical Portuguese word for skilled, not a Japanese form.
A separate suiren is paraphrased as midori no teguruma, a green or ornamented carriage. The Portuguese offers carriage and litter as alternatives.
Andas, completed from an-, means a litter or carrying chair; bem ornadas characterizes these conveyances as richly ornamented.
This suiren refers to fine hanging blinds, paraphrased as midori no sudare. The initial is S, not the draft's B.

runs.text: ſe dependurão nas portas, ou varandas.

lines.note: The blinds are hung in doorways or verandas. Dependurão retains the historical Portuguese spelling and completes the relative clause begun above.
Suirin, literally a water wheel in the supplied Japanese paraphrase, is a wheel or noria used to raise water.
Rar completes tirar, so the definition specifies drawing or lifting water rather than merely a wheel located beside water.
Suiryoo is inference or conjecture, explained by oshihakaru. The scan restores the damaged headword's initial S and ui sequence.

Suiryoo suru, divided after Sui-, means to conjecture. The example's faint vowel mark is retained as a circumflex, independently from the headword's caron; the exact worn mark remains a nonblocking uncertainty.
Suiroo and roosui denote declining with age, paraphrased by otoroe and oitari. The intervening l is Latin vel, 'or', not Japanese.

runs.text: Velhice, ou aparencia de velho ja gaſtado.

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies old age or the appearance of an already worn-out old person, completing the preceding Japanese equivalents.
This separate suiroo is a tower or raised structure over water, as mizu no yagura indicates. Bai- begins the Portuguese architectural noun on the next row.
Baileu is completed across the line break and described as built over water. The scan reads agoa, not OCR atoa.
Suisan means presenting oneself uninvited, paraphrased by oshi-mairu. The scan supports Suiſan rather than the draft's malformed Saiſani.
Speaking without having been asked is the second application of the same unsolicited or presumptuous action, not an unrelated definition.
Suisat is inference or conjecture, explained by oshi-miru. The meaningful ſ/f confusion is resolved as ſ; the final t is a historical checked coda, not a missing syllable.
This completes Suisat suru, to infer or conjecture. It is the continuation of the preceding example rather than a new headword.
Suisoo means aquatic vegetation, literally mizu-kusa in the Japanese paraphrase. No final punctuation has been supplied to regularize the short gloss.
Suison is water damage or loss caused by water. The Japanese paraphrase uses son for damage, not a separate object associated with water.
The relative clause identifies water as the cause of the damage or loss. The subject follows the Portuguese verb.
Suitai is paraphrased through green-dark eyebrow pigment, while the Portuguese extends it to a beautiful face or countenance.
The gloss completes the beautiful-countenance sense. The example pairs suitai with koogan, a rosy face, before a comparison with flowers.
Hana, divided after fa-, supplies the flowers in the comparison; komayaka nari characterizes the rich or delicate beauty. The Portuguese starts 'a face more beautiful'.
Bello is completed across the break, and the face is said to be rosier than roses. The printed Portuguese accent is retained.
This homonymous suitai means green moss, explicitly midori no koke, and is distinct from the preceding beauty vocabulary.
Suitei is the bottom of a body of water; mizu no soko and fundo dagoa give corresponding Japanese and Portuguese explanations.
Suiteki denotes playing the flute, explained through fuku fue. Frauta is preserved as the historical Portuguese spelling.
Suitoo denotes the water's edge, paraphrased as mizu no hotori. The circumflex is preserved rather than assimilated to neighboring caroned headwords.
Suiton is identified only as a particular dish. The brief historical gloss is not expanded into a modern recipe.
Suion means the sound of water, as mizu no oto confirms. The source's voto and Portuguese soido remain diplomatic spellings.
Suishaku is explained by ato wo taruru, with the Portuguese describing a kami or Buddha acting in another's place. Cami occurs inside the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Fotoque em lugar de outro, ou com differente

lines.note: Fotoque is the Japanese religious term hotoke embedded in the Portuguese sentence. The definition concerns substitution or manifestation under another identity.

runs.text: nome fazendo officio do primeiro comoguardã-

lines.note: The manifestation bears a different name while performing the original figure's office. Guardã- begins guardando, the act of protecting the place.
Completes guardando aquelle lugar, guarding that place. This belongs to the religious definition rather than the following water-purity entry.
The entry prefers seisui to suisei for pure, clean water. Potiùs is Latin 'rather' and is wholly italic, unlike the surrounding Japanese forms.
Sensui is preferred to suisen and paraphrased as mizu no izumi, a water spring. The OCR's fragmented Porùs is corrected to the printed Potiùs.
The Portuguese identifies a spring of water, completing the preceding entry and distinguishing it from the food name that follows.

runs.text: Certa iguaria feita da raiz de hũa erua.

lines.note: This suisen is a dish made from a herb's root. The headword has an abbreviation mark over e; the scan restores S and iguaria rather than OCR Fuixe and iguria.
Suisenkwa is identified as a flower of that name. The initial of Flor is F, not OCR H; rosa here need not imply a modern rose species.
Suishoo denotes being on or above water, explicitly mizu no ue. The printed vye is retained as the historical spelling.
A distinct suishoo means crystal or glass. Its identical romanized shape does not make it a continuation of the preceding spatial expression.
Suishoku is the color of water, paraphrased as mizu no iro. The next entry supplies a different homonymous color expression.
This suishoku denotes green, as midori no iro specifies. The final upright S is the dictionary's written-language label, not part of the italic gloss.
Suishu is glossed with the historical Portuguese term for dropsy. The scan supports Hydropeſia, correcting the draft's Hodropeſia without modernizing the spelling.
This suishu means sailors or seamen. It is a separate homonym, not a continuation of the preceding illness term.

runs.text: Certa flor, ou bonina do Outono.

lines.note: Suiyoohi is described as a particular autumn flower. The gloss does not provide enough botanical detail to identify a species securely.
Sujit means many days; kazu and hi explain its components. The final t is preserved as the historical checked ending.

runs.text: Muitas dezenas de annos tè cento.

lines.note: Sujuunen means several tens of years, described as extending up to a hundred. Annos has two n types, not the OCR's nx.

runs.text: Muitas dezenas de dias tè cento.

lines.note: Sujuunichi gives the corresponding quantity in days. The extra i in the draft's Sujǔinichi is not present in the scan.

runs.text: Muitas dezenas de homẽs tè cento.

lines.note: Sujuunin counts several tens of people. Its damaged headword is supported by the visible ending and the parallel years and days entries immediately above.
Sumai first means dwelling or residing, illustrated by sumai suru. The italic item marker introduces the second, architectural sense below.
The second sense concerns the manner of building or laying out houses. It explains the following example of a well-designed residence.
Sumai no yoi ie means a house with a good arrangement or design, directly matched by casa bem traçada.

runs.text: Estar a caſa bem, ou mal lã-

lines.note: This verb describes a house being well or badly laid out. The principal parts and their vowel marks are preserved as printed.
Yo(o) sumoota ie illustrates a well-designed house. The example's marked o is visible despite abrasion; ca- begins the repeated Portuguese casa.
Completes casa bem traçada, translating the example rather than introducing another headword.
This homonymous verb concerns sailing close to the wind. Abolinar is supported by the printed rounded vowel and the next line's bolina phrase.
Sumaini and sumoote hashiru are alternatives for sailing on a bowline or close-hauled. The initial l is the alternative marker.
Suman denotes many tens of thousands; sumannin applies that quantity to people. The Portuguese initially says many thousands and specifies the counting unit below.

runs.text: Muitos milhares de homes contando de dez mil

lines.note: The count is explicitly made in units of ten thousand people. The unexpanded homes is retained rather than supplied with an assumed nasal abbreviation.
Por diante completes 'from ten thousand onward'. The initial d is visible, correcting the OCR's ciante.
Sumashi, sumasu is transitive clearing or clarifying. The example begins mizu wo sumasu, making water clear; ſu corrects the meaningful f/ſ confusion.
Masu completes the water-clearing example. The figurative application then begins ri wo, introducing the clarification of a reason or principle.
Ri wo sumasu means making the reason clear or manifest. The scan supports ſumaſu and razão, not the OCR's ſumaru and vazão.
Kokoro wo sumasu is purifying and calming the heart. The printed paragraph mark and initial Co restore material damaged in the draft.
After completing pacificar, kuji wo sumasu introduces settling or adjudicating a lawsuit. A- begins the Portuguese verb on the next row.

runs.text: ueriguar a demanda. ¶ Este verbo junto à

lines.note: Aueriguar completes the lawsuit gloss; the e is heavily abraded but its position and the surviving word support the reading. The next explanation concerns attaching this verb to another verb's stem.

runs.text: raiz de outros ſignifica acabarſe, ou fazerſe bẽ

lines.note: As a second verb after another stem, sumasu conveys completion or doing something thoroughly and well. The tilde in bẽ is not expanded.
Kikisumasu illustrates attentive or thorough listening. The visible gap after capital Q is retained in Q iqiſumaſu; bem corrects the draft's hem.
Inteiramente completes the listening gloss. The next sense is paying debts, with a visible plural ending in diuidas.
Oimono wo sumasu illustrates settling a debt. The vowel after V is abraded; Voimonouo is preferred to OCR Vuimonouo from its remaining rounded outline and the debt context.
The dictionary next records washing as women's vocabulary. Kami wo begins the example concerning washing the head or hair; Vt is italic apparatus.

runs.text: Lauar a cabeça, ou os cabellos.

lines.note: Kami wo sumasu completes the example and is translated as washing the head or hair. It is not the homonymous paper-making use found later.
Sume, sumuru, sumeta is given as concluding or settling a matter. The scan ends in the example marker Vt with punctuation, not a hyphen.
Sanyoo wo sumuru means settling the accounts. The Portuguese specifies payment, with pagã- continued by do on the next row.
The accounts are settled by paying everything. Ri wo sumuru then supplies the figurative example of clarifying a reason or principle.
Rar completes aclarar, to clarify. At the far right, xo dagoa belongs to the next entry's divided baixo dagoa, not to the reason gloss; its physical displacement is preserved.
This sumu means diving or swimming underwater. Bai- continues in the displaced xo dagoa printed at the preceding row's right edge; OCR bal- confused i with l.
This distinct sumu is intransitive: water becomes clear. The following continuation extends the verb to completion or settlement.

runs.text: Concluirſe, ou acabarſe. ¶ Itẽ, Per met,

lines.note: After 'be concluded or finished', the figurative example begins ri. The Japanese Ri- and its terminal hyphen are roman, separate from the italic apparatus.
Ri ga sunda is explained as 'it is clear'. Ri no sumanu then begins a contrasting negative example, divided after suma-.
Ri no sumanu koto ja describes something unreasonable or not justified. The negative nu completes the verb from the preceding row.
Another sumu means dwelling or inhabiting. It is a separate homonym from clearing and underwater swimming.
Sumi is ink. The example here concerns a carpenter applying an ink mark, as the next row specifies, rather than the later ink-grinding example.

runs.text: ſinal o carpinteiro no pao, ou madeira. ¶

lines.note: The carpenter marks a piece of wood. The final Su- begins Sumiuo ſuri on the next page; the catchword miuo repeats the anticipated continuation and is not running text.
